views.note: the container validates the bearer token; the tenant arrives as a validated claim

views.label: Transaction
views.note: the use case owns the JTA transaction; the tenant predicate and the RLS policy both apply

views.label: Response
views.note: a DTO record crosses the API — never the entity

segments.label: The use case owns the transaction

messages.label: SET app.tenant_id · SELECT … WHERE id AND tenant_id

cards.title: The edge stays thin
items: the resource parses, validates, calls one use case and maps the Result — no business rule, no EntityManager, no @Transactional on the resource
the tenant arrives as a value (a TenantId), not as a SecurityContext the use case could read; a use case never sees HttpServletRequest, SecurityContext or a JMSContext
the tenant comes from the validated token — never from a query string and never from an unverified header

cards.title: Two lines of defence
items: the use case checks permission and ownership before the write and returns AppError.forbidden — the URL and the roles only shape the UX
the adapter sets app.tenant_id on the transaction before the first query, and the RLS policy with a non-bypass application role filters again
a missing predicate yields zero rows, never a cross-tenant read; the two-tenant test is a release blocker

cards.title: The response
items: a DTO record crosses the API, never the JPA entity: no lazy proxy, no over-posting, no internal id
the envelope is { "error": { code, message, requiredPermission, correlationId } }; one ExceptionMapper per family maps to 401/403/404/409/422/429/5xx
a version mismatch is a typed conflict (409), not a 500 — and a stack trace, SQL text or an internal id never leaves the server
